issues.legal_issue: A court exercising writ jurisdiction may not reappraise evidence and substitute its own conclusion for a lower court’s factual finding on comparative hardship.
material_facts: The prescribed authority considered evidence about the comparative hardship of the landlord and tenant and found the landlord’s need greater.
The District Judge affirmed that finding on appeal.
The High Court treated the comparative-need finding as one of fact and declined to disturb it in writ proceedings.
The challenge before the Supreme Court was that the High Court had not itself examined comparative hardship.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right not to reappraise the evidence or substitute its own conclusion for the factual finding affirmed by the District Judge; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court does not reappraise evidence to reach a conclusion different from that of the Prescribed Authority or the District Judge on a factual question such as comparative hardship. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_factual_findi: A party challenges a factual finding in proceedings seeking writ review of a lower authority’s decision.
predicates.comparative_hardship_assessed_on_evidenc: The lower authority assesses the parties’ comparative hardship on the evidence and makes a finding.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_affirmed_finding: A lower appellate court affirms the factual finding.

issues.definition: When writ proceedings challenge a factual finding on comparative hardship that was based on evidence and affirmed on appeal, the High Court does not reappraise the evidence to reach its own conclusion.
